hints: The stone starts from rest, so its initial velocity is zero.
Use the constant-acceleration displacement relationship with s = 36 m and a = g.
walkthrough: Take downward as positive. The stone is released from rest, so u = 0, and its displacement to the water is s = 36 m.
For constant gravitational acceleration, s = ut + ½at² becomes 36 = ½(9.81)t².
Thus t = √(2 × 36 / 9.81) = 2.71... s, so the fall time is 2.7 s.

ai_rubric.observable: Uses a constant-acceleration relation for a 36 m fall from rest with g = 9.81 m s⁻².
Obtains a fall time of 2.7 s.

hints: Separate the stone's fall time from the interval the student actually times.
Consider the release, the stopwatch, and the signal that tells the student to stop it.
walkthrough: The calculation in part (a) is only the stone's fall time, whereas the stopwatch runs until the splash is heard.
The sound of the splash needs time to travel up the well, so the measured interval can include an additional delay after impact.
Human reaction time when stopping the stopwatch can also lengthen the recorded interval.
A mismatch between releasing the stone and starting the stopwatch, a stopwatch calibration offset, or a non-zero initial stone speed are further valid reasons for a different recorded time.

ai_rubric.observable: States any three distinct valid procedural, timing, signal-travel, apparatus or model-assumption reasons why the stopwatch interval differs from the calculated fall time.

hints: For precision, compare the repeated values with one another rather than with 36.0 m.
For accuracy, compare the cluster of repeated values with the known true depth.
walkthrough: The three calculated depths range only from 53.9 m to 54.4 m, a spread of 0.5 m, so they are close together.
Close agreement among repeated values means the readings are precise.
However, all three values are about 54 m, whereas the true depth is 36.0 m, so the results are far from the true value.
Because accuracy is closeness to the true value, the results are not accurate.

ai_rubric.observable: Explains that the repeated depth values are closely grouped or have little scatter.
Explains that the repeated values are far from the true depth of 36.0 m.
